title: The p-n junction and the diode's I–V curve: why current flows one way
examples: How does a p-n junction diode work?
Why does a silicon diode turn on at 0.7 V?
How do I calculate current through a diode and resistor?

parts.label: R
parts.ask: What is the constant-voltage diode model?

explain.say: Every phone charger, solar panel and LED relies on one simple device that lets current flow in only one direction: the diode. Inside it is a p-n junction, where p-type silicon meets n-type. On the board, a 5 volt supply pushes current through a 430 ohm resistor and a silicon diode.

draw.text: The p-n junction and the diode's I–V curve: why current flows one way

parts.label: R
parts.ask: What is the constant-voltage diode model?

explain.say: At the junction, electrons from the n side wander across and fill holes on the p side. That leaves a thin layer with no free carriers at all, the depletion region, and a built-in voltage across it, like a small hill. To get current flowing you must push the p side positive enough to flatten that hill. What do you think happens if you push the other way?

parts.label: R
parts.ask: What is the constant-voltage diode model?

draw.text: Depletion region: no free carriers, and a built-in barrier.

explain.say: The hill grows, and almost nothing flows. Here's the diode's I–V curve, current against voltage. Below about 0.6 volts, hardly any current. Then the curve shoots up: by 0.7 volts several milliamps flow, and by 0.75 volts about 40. That bend is the knee. The rise is exponential: every extra 60 millivolts multiplies the current by about ten. Where would you say the diode turns on?

curves.label: Silicon diode
curves.ask: Why is the turn-on voltage of a silicon diode 0.7 V?

explain.say: Around 0.7 volts, the knee. Now flip the diode round, which is called reverse bias. The depletion region widens, and only a tiny leakage current of nanoamps flows. The diode is a one-way valve. Push hard enough in reverse, though, and it breaks down, which a special diode, the Zener, uses on purpose. Why might a one-way valve help in a charger?

explain.say: To turn AC into DC, coming soon! Now the worked example. Engineers model a silicon diode as a fixed 0.7 volt drop once it is on. So the resistor gets 5 minus 0.7, which is 4.3 volts, and the current is 4.3 over 430 ohms, 10 milliamps, just as the ammeter reads. Well done! Challenge: what resistor gives 20 milliamps from the same 5 volts?

faq.a: The boundary where p-type and n-type silicon meet in one crystal. Carriers cross and recombine there, leaving a depletion region with a built-in voltage that lets current flow easily only one way.
asks: What happens at a pn junction?

faq.a: A thin layer either side of the junction that has lost its free electrons and holes. It acts as an insulating barrier with a built-in voltage.

faq.q: Why is the turn-on voltage of a silicon diode 0.7 V?
faq.a: The current rises exponentially with voltage. Below about 0.6 volts it is tiny; by about 0.7 volts it reaches the milliamps real circuits use, so 0.7 volts is the practical knee.

faq.q: What is the constant-voltage diode model?
faq.a: Treat the diode as off below 0.7 volts and as a fixed 0.7 volt drop when on. It makes hand calculations quick and is usually accurate to a few percent.
asks: How do I calculate current through a diode?

faq.q: What happens when a diode is reverse biased?
faq.a: The depletion region widens and only a tiny leakage current flows, nanoamps for a small silicon diode, until the voltage reaches breakdown.
asks: Does current flow backwards through a diode?

facts: William Shockley derived the ideal diode equation in 1949.
A forward-biased silicon diode typically drops about 0.6 to 0.7 volts, while a red LED drops about 1.8 to 2 volts.

quiz.say: A 9 volt battery drives a silicon diode and an 830 ohm resistor in series. What current flows?
quiz.show: A 9 V battery drives a silicon diode and an 830 Ω resistor in series. What current flows?
quiz.why: The resistor gets 9 minus 0.7, which is 8.3 volts, and 8.3 over 830 is 10 milliamps.

wrong.1: That forgets the 0.7 volt diode drop.
wrong.2: That divides only the diode drop by the resistor.

quiz.say: A silicon diode is reverse biased by 5 volts. What is the current, roughly?
quiz.show: A silicon diode is reverse biased by 5 V. The current is about...
quiz.why: In reverse the depletion region widens and only a tiny leakage current flows.

wrong.1: Milliamps flow only in forward bias, above the knee.
wrong.2: Current only rises sharply at reverse breakdown, far above 5 volts for an ordinary diode.
